Brannock Sedge.narrative: I've run my cart of salt and dried fish along this shore since I was old enough to push it, and I know every stall-keeper from the tide steps to the far end of the market. The quay buys fish and sells it back to itself twice before noon, and I take my share in the middle of that, honestly enough. Mara Quell's stall fee is due and I'll pay it when the cart comes back full, not before. Bramwell Tallow can have the rope trade; I'll keep the salt.
values: a fair price, paid and taken
the quay looks after its own
goals: clear the stall fee owed to Mara Quell
keep the salt-fish trade with the Reedmoor reed-cutters steady
see the seawall built so the lower quay trades again
buy a second cart so the Reedmoor run doesn't cost me the morning stalls
learn to read the ledger figures Mara Quell keeps, so I know what I'm owed to the mark

relations.name: Dory Sedge
relations.label: wife
relations.note: She smokes it, I sell it; we've never needed to say which of us is the better trader.

relations.name: Tam Sedge
relations.label: son
relations.note: Good lad in the shed, but he won't go near the harbour after dark and I don't push him.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: Warden
relations.note: She holds the stall fee over me like a net over a fish. I owe it; I'll pay it.

relations.name: Bramwell Tallow
relations.label: rival
relations.note: He'd sell rope to a drowning man and charge him for the knot.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Her lamp oil and dried fish move well beside mine at the morning stalls.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Knows the price of everything on the quay, and most of the time she's right.

relations.name: Eadric Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: His reed-bed salt fish fills my cart cheap and never spoils.

relations.name: Ostrander Vane
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Patches the lower quay with salvage and swears at the Kettlebridge price. I'd do the same.

relations.name: Nell Sedge
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: The Reedmoor reed-cutters send salt fish through her; we've done well by it.

memories.gist: The night the surge came, I hauled my cart up the slip and watched the lower quay go under; I lost a season's salt in the water.
The morning I first took Eadric Sedge's salt fish on the cart and sold the lot before the bells.
Bramwell Tallow cornered the rope trade and told me to my face the cart men should stick to fish.
Tam was born in the room over the smoke shed and Dory was back at the stalls inside a week.

stances.why: A trader who doesn't pay his stall fee is a trader nobody sells to.
The lower quay went under once; it will go under again, and my cart with it.
They send us stone at a price that keeps the wall unbuilt, and call it trade.
Everything I own keeps because I salt it and wait; that's the whole of my trade.

pastimes: walking the tide steps at low water, checking what the sea has left
dicing with the other carters at the back of the market when the day's trade is done
telling the old wreck stories to whoever's drinking at the stall
Brannock Sedge.calling: I'm a carter, and a good one: salt and dried fish up and down this shore, and no load spoiled under my tarpaulin yet.

Dory Sedge.narrative: I've smoked fish in the shed behind the market for near twenty years, and the morning stalls know my smoke by the smell of it. Brannock carts what I smoke and I keep the shed and the boy and the fire. The cough goes round the poor terrace every winter and I've buried neighbours from it. I'd feed the whole quay if the shed held more.
values: feed people before you count marks
the poor terrace is still the quay
goals: keep the smoke shed and the morning stall paying
see the winter cough off the poor terrace
keep Tam out of the night harbour
learn to smoke a new cure that keeps through the summer heat
see Tam learn his letters, even if I never did

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: husband
relations.note: He carts and haggles; I smoke and keep the fire. It's worked this long.

relations.name: Tam Sedge
relations.label: son
relations.note: He's a good hand in the shed and I won't have him feared into the dark water.

relations.name: Nia Brine
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: We trade oil for smoke and worry over the same coughs.

relations.name: Maren Vane
relations.label: healer
relations.note: When the cough takes the terrace, she's the one I send for.

relations.name: Mira Sallow
relations.label: healer
relations.note: Her herbs and salves have kept more than one shed family through a winter.

relations.name: Mara Quell
relations.label: Warden
relations.note: She wants the wall; I want the poor terrace fed. Both can be true.

relations.name: Ilse Ostrander
relations.label: neighbour
relations.note: Her noodle stall buys my smoked fish and never once haggled me down.

relations.name: Perrin Tallow
relations.label: trade partner
relations.note: Sharp on price, but she'll lend you her apron if yours is burning.

relations.name: Tam Sedge's friend Dory Gull
relations.label: child's friend
relations.note: She's a good child and Tam plays with her; I keep an eye on them both by the water.

memories.gist: The surge took the shed roof and half the smoke racks; I rebuilt the racks from salvage before the fish rotted.
Tam was small when the cough went round the terrace, and I sat up nights with the neighbours' children as well as my own.
The first morning my smoked fish sold out at the stall before the sun was over the masts.
Nia Brine and I split a barrel of lamp oil when neither of us had the marks for a whole one.

stances.why: I've seen what an empty pot does to a house, and the seawall won't fill it.
My name is on every fish I sell at the morning stalls.
Wolves and stone prices don't kill half so many on this quay as the winter cough.
The harbour at night took my uncle and I'll not have it take Tam.

pastimes: singing the old harbour songs while the racks smoke
tending a few pots of herbs behind the shed
sitting on the step at dusk with Brannock and a cup of something warm
Dory Sedge.calling: I smoke fish, and I'd have it no other way: slow smoke, fresh sell, and the shed smelling right by dawn.

Tam Sedge.narrative: I help Mam in the smoke shed, turning the racks and keeping the fire low, and I know the smell of fish smoke better than I know my letters. Da lets me ride the cart sometimes when it goes no further than the morning stalls. I don't like the harbour when it's dark; the water makes noises like breathing. Dory Gull and me play under the stalls where the lamps don't reach.
goals: be trusted with the whole smoke rack
not go down to the harbour at night
be trusted with the whole smoke rack by myself
learn to swim so the dark water isn't so frightening

relations.name: Dory Sedge
relations.label: mother
relations.note: She lets me keep the fire low and says I've a good hand for it.

relations.name: Brannock Sedge
relations.label: father
relations.note: He lets me ride the cart when it's only the morning stalls.

relations.name: Dory Gull
relations.label: friend
relations.note: We play under the stalls where the lamps don't reach.

relations.name: Sable Harrow
relations.label: stallkeeper
relations.note: She gave me a mark to carry a crate and didn't say what was in it.

memories.gist: The night the water came over the lower quay, Da carried me up the slip and Mam's shed roof came off.
The first time Mam let me turn the racks by myself and the fish came out brown and sweet.

stances.why: It makes noises like breathing and I stay up by the lamps.
She says a low fire smokes sweet, and she's never wrong about fish.

pastimes: playing under the stalls with Dory Gull where the lamps don't reach
turning the smoke racks and being trusted with the fire
riding the cart as far as the morning stalls
Tam Sedge.calling: When I'm big I want to run the smoke shed like Mam, or maybe drive the cart like Da.
